problem: Saying a maintenance-free battery 'is not sealed against all pressure; most have a valve' mixes two different products. A flooded maintenance-free (low-water-loss) battery is simply vented; a pressure-relief valve is the defining feature of VRLA (AGM/gel) batteries, which the chapter itself explains two paragraphs later. A student will conclude that every maintenance-free battery is a VRLA.
fix: A maintenance-free battery limits water loss so it needs no periodic topping-up. Flooded maintenance-free types are vented through small vents. Only valve-regulated types (AGM, gel) carry a pressure-relief valve.

problem: 'Replace some antimony with calcium' is loose. Standard lead-calcium grids use essentially no antimony; antimony is removed (or kept very low in hybrid designs) and calcium is added to the alloy.
fix: Lead-calcium grids replace the antimony of conventional grids with calcium (hybrid designs keep a little antimony in one plate). Calcium reduces gassing and self-discharge, so less water is lost.

problem: 12.0 V on a rested battery is roughly a quarter charge, not 'deeply discharged'; calling it deep discharge exaggerates and hides the 12.2 V half-charge step.
fix: A full 12 V battery reads about 12.6 V to 12.8 V, 12.2 V about half charge, and 12.0 V about a quarter charge; below roughly 11.9 V it is deeply discharged.

problem: 'Measure the bus' is jargon an ESL reader will not follow; the quantity to measure is not named.
fix: Charging-system test: run the engine at fast idle and measure the voltage across the battery terminals; about 13.8 V to 14.4 V shows the alternator is charging.

problem: The figure says 'same load' but never states the current, and a good battery held above 10.5 V for 600 min at 25 A would give 250 Ah, far beyond any car battery. Without a stated current the curve cannot be tied to the reserve-capacity definition just taught.
fix: State the load in the caption, for example: 'Same 25 A load, two 60 Ah batteries: the good battery stays above 10.5 V to about 120 min, the weak one crosses 10.5 V much earlier.' Adjust the plotted times to match.

problem: 'Do not load-test a sealed AGM below its safe voltage' is vague; the student is not told what the safe limit is, and the point is really about depth of discharge, not about the test itself.
fix: Do not discharge an AGM battery below about 10.5 V during a load test (and never open a VRLA battery); deep discharge shortens its life.
